episodes.172157: The break in the monsoon activity in early September came to an end as Hurricane Kay went up the coast of Baja California and southern California. While Kay remained well off to the west of New Mexico, it was responsible for moisture advection into the area which led to an increase in thunderstorm activity on September 9, 2022. Strong thunderstorms developed over the northern mountains during the evening hours and propagated southward thanks to strong outflow boundaries. Winds associated with these outflow boundaries were severe as measured by weather stations in Stanley and Golden.
episodes.172179: The Calf Canyon burn scar had received a well deserved break from flash flooding impacts for a couple of weeks at the end of August and into early September. However, monsoon season was not officially over yet, and a return of moisture resulted in numerous thunderstorms developing across the area on September 10, 2022. Unfortunately, the Calf Canyon burn scar was impacted as a nearly stationary thunderstorms dropped over two inches of rain on the southern portion of the large burn scar which caused flash flooding in the area.
episodes.172265: Moisture from Tropical Storm Kay which was centered just off the Baja coast surged northward into central California during the morning of September 10. While the deeper moisture remained to the south and east of central California, enough moisture made it into the area and combined with an unstable airmass left over the area in the wake of a heat wave that persisted for several days over the region. Widespread showers and scattered thunderstorms fired up across the area during the afternoon of September 10 and moved rapidly toward the northwest. The rapid movement of the thunderstorms inhibited flooding potential, but several locations in the higher Sierra Nevada and the Tehachapi Mountains picked up between a quarter to a half inch of rainfall. Amounts in the San Joaquin Valley and the Kern County Desert areas generally ranged from a trace to a few hundredths of an inch of rainfall with the most noticeable impacts being from outflow winds from some of the stronger cells over the Sierra Nevada.

episodes.173083: Downpours occurred over a portion of leeward Haleakala in East Maui with afternoon heating, leading to flash flooding on the 9th.  More showers developed later over parts of Oahu, Maui, and the Big Island.  No serious injuries or property damage were reported.
episodes.173277: Pre-frontal and sea breeze storms produced some wind damage ahead of a strengthening upper level low across the MS River Valley.  High moisture, bulk shear of 30-40 kts and elevated surface CAPEs produced some strong to severe storms.

episodes.173846: Scattered strong summer storms resulted in gusty winds in excess of 34 knots across portions of the coastal waters.
episodes.174042: Moisture continued to flow northward across northern Arizona as the weakening remnants of Kay were post-tropical and located southwest of San Diego. The low level moisture |brought showers and thunderstorms to the area.
episodes.174068: Tropical Cyclone Kay formed on September 4th, 2022 and made its closest approach to Southern California on the 9th and 10th, with the center of Kay coming within 120 miles of San Diego. Tropical moisture associated with Kay managed to produce heavy rainfall leading to flooding across mountainous terrain in Southern California on September 9th and 10th. This led to a number of wind damage and flooding events in the mountains and desert foothill locations in Southern California. Kay transitioned to a Post-Tropical Cyclone that weekend, but left enough lingering moisture to support additional rounds of heavy thunderstorms through the 11th and 12th of September. These later rounds of heavy rain would lead to multiple significant debris flow events in the San Bernardino County Mountains, namely in and around the Apple and El Dorado burn scars.
episodes.174069: As Hurricane Earl continued to lift well north of the islands, moisture was still being pulled from the Caribbean into the islands. Therefore, the active weather period continued.
episodes.174079: Slow moving thunderstorms produced very heavy rain that led to flooding in northwest Florida.
episodes.174163: Tropical Storm Kay moving northward just west of Baja California pushed deep tropical moisture towards southern CA, where objective analysis showed PWATs in excess of 2 inches. Bands of moderate to heavy rainfall associated with the outer bands from the tropical storm affected most of Imperial County, resulting in significant flash flooding.
episodes.174189: Broad southeast flow associated with the circulation of Tropical Storm Kay, which was located just west of the Baja California Peninsula, set up across Arizona. This helped in advecting moisture into the area with PWAT's in excess of 1.5. Instability was also present with MLCAPE values of around 1000 J/KG. In addition, there was upper-level diffluence over south-central Arizona, which helped enhance the shower and thunderstorm activity.
episodes.174201: Waterspouts were observed just off the coast during the morning and early afternoon hours.
episodes.174525: Isolated thunderstorms developed across the South Carolina coastal waters in the early morning hours and moved onshore along the Charleston County coast. These thunderstorms developed near a stationary front where there was enough shear, helicity, and instability to produce rotation. One thunderstorm produced a brief tornado as it moved onshore in Charleston County.
episodes.174600: A tropical airmass interacted with a stalled frontal zone across portions of the southern Coatal Plain and eastern Sandhills of central North Carolina, producing heavy rain from numerous showers and storms. Flash flooding was reported in these areas, where the heaviest rain fell.

events.narrative: About 6 inches approximately of flowing water was observed across Dolphin Drive in Salton City. No damages or injuries were reported.

Several roads that intersect Waterman Wash in the Rainbow Valley/Buckeye area were impassable/closed due to flooding. This included Riggs Road, Tuthill Road between between Pecos Road and Fairview Street, and Narramore Road between Dean Road and Airport Road. A Flood Control District of Maricopa County Gauge of Waterman Wash at Rainbow Valley Road reported a peak flow of 6.12 feet (1151 cfs), which was 2.82 feet above alarm stage. No damages or injuries were reported.

SR-238 was closed in its entirety between Gila Bend and SR-347 due to significant flooding. The Maricopa Fire and Medical Crew as well as the Goodyear Fire Department in a collective effort had to rescue approximately 32 people in stranded vehicles. No injuries were reported.
Thunderstorm outflow winds caused a 65 mph wind gust at a public weather station near Golden.
Thunderstorm outflow winds caused a 67 mph wind gust measured by a public weather station near Stanley.
Heavy rain caused several streets to be closed due to flooding.

A NWS storm survey team confirmed that a brief EF-0 tornado occurred near Highway 17 in Mount Pleasant. The weak and short-lived tornado touched down on Zacoma Drive and traveled north-northwest and dissipated near the intersection of Highway 17 and Lieben Road. Damage was mostly confined to small trees and large limbs, but there was some minor roof damage to a Mount Pleasant Public Works building off of Lieben Road. Damage was limited to a small area along Zacoma Drive, Ty Lane, Tower Drive, and Lieben Road. The damage pattern in this area was consistent with an EF-0 tornado with maximum estimated winds around 70 mph.

A nearly stationary thunderstorm over El Porvenir produced over two inches of rainfall on this area of the Calf Canyon burn scar. This caused flash flooding on Beaver Creek and Gallinas Creek with significant debris found on Highway 65. The IMET on duty found several locations along Highway 65 that were covered in tree debris, rocks, and mud. Some buildings along the roadway were inundated with a couple of feet of water. The IMET also noted that water had threatened homes in the area as well, but these homes seemed to have been protected with sandbagging. Damages are estimated.
